question: What does a critique and Boy Scout refactoring of a well-written real module (JUnit's ComparisonCompactor) look like step by step?
contributions: A worked refactoring of ComparisonCompactor from Listing 15-2 to 15-5, annotating each step with smell/heuristic codes (N1, N4, N6, N7, G9, G11, G28-G33).

results.claim: Refactoring is iterative trial and error, and later steps can undo earlier ones.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: Refactoring is an iterative process full of trial and error, inevitably converging on something that we feel is worthy of a professional.

results.claim: The tests give 100 percent coverage of the original module, which the author takes as high confidence it works.
results.setup: Coverage run on original ComparisonCompactor with the 20-odd tests of Listing 15-1; the chapter does not name the coverage tool or say line vs branch
results.note: Next sentence: Every line of code, every if statement and for loop, is executed by the tests.

results.claim: Removing the +1 offsets exposed a condition that was dead code: with the old 1-based suffix, the if could never be false.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: Before we made the change, the if statement was nonfunctional because suffixIndex could never be less than one!

results.claim: Both guarding ifs in compactString were commented out and the tests still passed, so they were deleted.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: So let’s comment them out and run the tests. They passed!

results.claim: Hidden temporal coupling between findCommonPrefix and findCommonSuffix is better exposed by merging them into one function than by passing a dummy argument.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: The passing of the prefixIndex argument is a bit arbitrary [G32].

results.claim: A function named compact hid the side effect of an error check and returned a formatted message, so it was renamed formatCompactedComparison.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: So naming this function compact hides the side effect of the error check.

results.claim: Negated conditionals are slightly harder to understand than positives, so the guard was inverted.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: Negatives are slightly harder to understand than positives [G29].

results.claim: Member-variable f prefixes are redundant in modern environments and were removed.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: Today’s environments make this kind of scope encoding redundant.

results.claim: The Boy Scout Rule: leave the module cleaner than found, even when authors did excellent work.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: each of us has the responsibility to leave the code a little better than we found it.

results.claim: The final structure groups analysis functions first and synthesis functions last, topologically sorted so each definition follows its use.
results.setup: ComparisonCompactor (JUnit), Java, one module refactored by the author
results.quote: The module is separated into a group of analysis func-

results.claim: The test file covers edge cases (nulls, overlaps, equal strings, a regression test named for bug 609972) with one assertion per tiny test; the author asks whether they could be simpler.

limits: One Java module of about 60 lines; no measurement beyond one coverage figure.
Heuristic codes (G, N) refer to Clean Code ch. 17, which is not in this PDF.
Final listing is shown only as a result; 'the rest of the changes' are not walked through (p. 263).
Java 2008 idioms (f prefixes, JUnit 3 TestCase) have dated.
practices: Read the tests first to learn the requirements (p. 252).
Check coverage of the tests before refactoring (p. 254).
Extract an encapsulated conditional into a named method (pp. 257-258).
Name functions for all they do, including side effects (p. 258).
Make temporal coupling explicit, and make it obvious why the order matters rather than passing an arbitrary argument (pp. 259-260).
Rerun tests after each change, and try deleting suspicious code to see if tests still pass (p. 262).
Expect to reverse earlier refactoring decisions (p. 264).
